analysis.one_liner: Taxes private fund managers' profit share as ordinary income instead of at lower capital gains rates.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax fund managers' carried interest as ordinary income was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture fund managers are typically paid with a share of their fund's profits, called carried interest. Under current law that pay is taxed at the lower capital gains rate (up to 20%) instead of the top income tax rate (37%) that applies to wages. This bill would reclassify that income as ordinary income, make it subject to Medicare and Social Security self-employment taxes, tax the gain when managers sell their fund stakes, and raise the penalty for misreporting it. The bill never received a committee hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: fund managers would pay ordinary income rates (up to 37% plus self-employment taxes) on pay they currently receive at the 20% capital gains rate, reducing the deficit or easing tax burdens on everyone else. Estimates cited in past debates put the revenue at billions of dollars a year, concentrated among a few thousand of the highest-earning Americans.

how_it_helps.text: It treats the 'carried interest' share of private equity and hedge fund managers' profits as ordinary income instead of lower-taxed capital gains, matching how wages are taxed.
It also taxes managers' share of dividends and small-business stock gains as ordinary income, closing related preferences.
It makes carried interest income subject to self-employment taxes (Medicare and Social Security), which it currently escapes.
It raises the penalty for underpaying tax by misclassifying this income to 40%.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital partners whose performance-based pay would be taxed at ordinary income rates up to 37% plus self-employment tax, and who would owe tax on partnership interests received for services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts 'qualified capital interests' — money the manager actually invests — and certain family partnerships, so some of the existing preference survives and the rules are complex to enforce.
Critics of closing the carried interest preference argue it could reduce incentives for investment management and shift some activity abroad; this concern was not tested in the record for this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a fairer tax code: people who manage other people's money would pay the same tax rates on their pay as everyone else pays on their wages, and wealthy households would still owe the lower capital gains rate on their own invested money. The main cost is the objection that changing the treatment of carried interest could affect how investment funds are structured and could modestly reduce new investment; the bill also allows exceptions for real capital contributed by managers and for family partnerships, which keep some of the existing preferences in place. Overall the bill is a straightforward tax increase on a small, high-income group, with the revenue available for public priorities or deficit reduction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended, so it never became law.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Pascrell Jr. introduced the bill on April 18, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never marked it up, and the House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity and hedge fund managers keep the lower capital gains tax rate on their performance-based pay, saving them the difference between capital gains and ordinary income rates. Because Ways and Means has jurisdiction over all tax bills, a single committee's decision not to act was enough to end the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.what_they_did: The private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital industry has consistently lobbied against carried interest tax increases in past Congresses, and similar proposals have repeatedly failed to reach a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and both cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans supported the bill.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Managers' performance-based compensation ('carried interest') would be taxed as ordinary income at top rates up to 37% rather than the 20% long-term capital gains rate, and would become subject to self-employment taxes. This is compensation for services, but under current law it is taxed as investment income.

High-income partners receiving partnership interests for services would pay tax on their value when received and could no longer use the section 1061 three-year holding rule (which the bill repeals) to qualify for lower rates. The tax savings currently flowing to this group would end.
